summary: Lists the messages that CCN's NETRJS server may send to a remote user, covering the initial connection, sign-on and sign-off. The messages explain problems such as busy ports and what to do about them.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 589 explains messages sent by the CCN NETRJS server during login and data transfer. It describes common timeouts, malformed transfer records and server failures, including when a user may retry or should report a problem.

subtitle: A guide to messages from the CCN NETRJS server.

tldr.problem: Remote users needed explanations of status and error messages from the CCN NETRJS service.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC groups messages into session setup, remote-site or network transfer failures, and CCN-side failures, and explains the conditions associated with them.
tldr.outcome: The guide helps users distinguish a refused session, a transfer problem that may be retried and a serious CCN failure to report.

today: RFC 589 is a message reference for the CCN NETRJS server, documenting its session and transfer notices.

sections.title: Connection, Sign-On and Sign-Off
sections.content: A refused Initial Connection Protocol request can mean that the NCP region has no free core or that CCN software is crashing. After connection, the server may report busy NETRJS ports or that RJS is not running; otherwise it sends a READY message asking the user to sign on. No operator input for 3 minutes causes sign-on timeout and session termination. An invalid sign-on can be re-entered. On sign-off, NETRJS waits for data transfers to finish before closing the Telnet connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The server reports whether a session can start and whether sign-on succeeds. If the user is inactive for 3 minutes, it closes the session; on sign-off it waits for transfers to finish.

sections.title: Remote-Site and Data-Transfer Errors
sections.content:
During data transfer, CCN closes a connection after 5 minutes without the expected activity, such as a printer or punch site failing to accept bits or a reader connection sending none. Header errors report conditions including a sequence mismatch, a length greater than 880 bytes, an unsupported type code or a fill-bit count not divisible by 8. A stream error can identify a faulty reader record, with codes describing issues such as truncated lines or malformed compressed text.

If a user aborts a transfer, the server sends a message identifying the device and terminal.
sections.plainLanguage: The server reports when a transfer is idle too long or its header or record is invalid. The message identifies the kind of problem so the remote user can decide whether to retry.

sections.title: CCN-Side Failures
sections.content:
A central operator can abort a NETRJS session. Other messages indicate serious CCN network-software problems and cause the session to be aborted; the RFC says these should be reported to CCN.

Some failures affect only a data-transfer process rather than the whole session. The data connection may be refused or terminated, and the user can try opening it again. Repeated failures should be reported.
sections.plainLanguage: Some CCN errors end the whole session and should be reported. Other errors stop only a transfer connection, which the user may try to open again.
